claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is a homogeneous, non-equilibrium metastable solid solution with Mg uniformly dissolved in the matrix.
The initial state contains no significant intermetallic precipitation.
The initial metastable state has optimal corrosion resistance.
The initial metastable state has optimal high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The metastable solid solution decomposes by diffusion-controlled precipitation.
Mg segregates from the initially uniform solid solution to energetically favorable sites.
Segregated Mg nucleates fine Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Isothermal aging at 400–600 °C increases the volume fraction of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates relative to the initial state.
Longer aging causes Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates to grow, coarsen, and coalesce.
Rapid quenching suppresses intermetallic precipitate formation and retains the metastable state.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates create regions that foster micro-galvanic corrosion.
Precipitate growth and coalescence disrupt formation of a uniform passivation layer.
Precipitate evolution alters high-temperature oxidation kinetics.
Aged samples have lower corrosion resistance than the rapidly quenched control.
Aged samples have lower high-temperature oxidation resistance than the rapidly quenched control.
The 400–600 °C interval represents critical service conditions for the proposed transformation and degradation process.
Exposure significantly outside 400–600 °C may activate additional transformation mechanisms.
